btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The interagency Quality Control Standards for Automated Valuation Models - finalized by FHFA, CFPB, and the banking regulators - are the first binding federal rules for the sector's core AI: the models that value homes in mortgage decisions.
points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.desc: The bureau's AVM rule page and its algorithmic-appraisal work are the record of how valuation bias and model accountability are supervised.
points.name: CFPB carries the consumer-protection side

points.desc: The National Association of Realtors' technology research tracks what AI tools agents and brokerages actually adopt.
points.name: NAR surveys the profession

points.desc: The Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation publishes the funding data on AI and proptech startups - the sector's investment barometer.
points.name: CRETI tracks proptech capital

points.desc: The Zestimate and the Redfin Estimate are the consumer-facing AVMs, each with published methodology and error rates - rare public documentation of production ML.
points.name: Zillow and Redfin publish their valuation models

points.desc: The iBuyer's pricing models carry real balance-sheet exposure - its own filings and documentation are the record of valuation AI with capital consequences.
points.name: Opendoor prices houses with models at risk

points.desc: JLL and CBRE - the commercial real estate services majors - deploy generative and predictive AI across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics.
points.name: The CRE giants run enterprise AI

points.desc: 3D capture and computer vision digitizing physical space - the data layer under virtual touring and property intelligence.
points.name: Matterport turns buildings into data

points.desc: EliseAI's leasing agents and AppFolio's property-management AI are where the sector's day-to-day automation ships.
points.name: Leasing and property ops are automating

points.desc: CREtech is the commercial proptech community and event network; MetaProp is the sector's dedicated venture firm publishing funding and sentiment research - together the clearest read on where proptech capital goes.
points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.desc: The Building Owners and Managers Association tracks AI in smart-building operations, energy efficiency, and predictive maintenance across commercial property.
points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

points.desc: The realtor association's technology accelerator is where residential proptech gets vetted and scaled - a window into which tools the profession is actually adopting.
points.name: NAR REACH backs the startups

points.desc: The residential brokerage's platform applies AI to agent workflows, client matching, and predictive listing recommendations.
points.name: Compass runs AI inside the brokerage workflow

points.desc: HouseCanary's valuation and forecasting models and Cherre's data integration layer are what institutional investors underwrite on - the wholesale side of the AVM story.
points.name: Institutional valuation runs on data platforms

points.desc: Prophia extracts terms, rent rolls, and obligations from commercial leases automatically - one of the clearest production uses of document AI in the sector.
points.name: Lease abstraction is a document-AI problem

points.desc: Visitt and Building Engines apply IoT sensing and machine learning to HVAC optimization, maintenance prediction, and tenant workflow in operating buildings.
points.name: Smart buildings close the operations loop

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
# Real Estate AI Deployment and Regulation

According to the Census Bureau's Business Time Use Survey, 28.9% of firms in the real estate and rental and leasing sector reported using AI in the two weeks prior to the latest survey, a marginal increase from 28.0% in the prior period. This adoption rate establishes real estate as a sector where AI use has become commonplace, though the data reflects only whether firms used AI tools at all, not depth or scope of deployment.

Automated valuation models sit at the center of the sector's AI infrastructure and regulatory attention. Zillow publishes Zestimates for over 110 million homes using neural network-based models that incorporate county records, tax assessor data, and MLS feeds across hundreds of data points per property. The Zestimate reflects the model's best estimate but can vary due to negotiation and changing market conditions, prompting Zillow to provide an estimated sales range alongside point estimates. Similarly, institutional investors rely on platforms like HouseCanary, which deliver AI-driven valuations and forecasts across 136 million U.S. properties. These models represent the production face of consumer and wholesale valuation. At the regulatory layer, the FHFA, CFPB, OCC, FRB, FDIC, and NCUA jointly adopted a final rule implementing quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers to determine collateral worth on mortgages secured by a consumer's principal dwelling. The rule mandates that institutions adopt policies, practices, procedures, and control systems ensuring AVMs adhere to quality control standards designed to guarantee high confidence in estimates, protect against data manipulation, seek to avoid conflicts of interest, and require random sample testing and reviews.

Beyond valuation, AI automates discrete operational workflows across residential and commercial property. Document-focused AI tools like Prophia extract lease terms and obligations from commercial leases automatically and combine AI extraction with expert validation to create structured lease data for risk mitigation and decision-making. EliseAI operates an agentic AI platform for housing and property management that handles messages, calls, and tasks automatically, integrating with existing systems to deliver 24/7 responses and scheduling while streaming complicated workflows. Building Engines' Prism platform delivers instant answers, recommendations, and automation to commercial property teams, enabling them to cut costs and grow NOI by working with data already in hand. Matterport's 3D capture and virtual tour software helps property managers digitize buildings, centralize management decisions across global portfolios, and reduce site visits by incorporating real-time data. These platforms concentrate on cost reduction and process acceleration rather than high-stakes decision-making, placing them outside the regulatory perimeter.

The sector's vendor landscape clusters around three tiers. At scale, commercial real estate giants like JLL report having invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, deploying intelligent systems across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics. Residential brokerages including Compass embed AI into agent workflows and predictive listing recommendations. Startup activity receives backing through NAR REACH, the National Association of Realtors' technology accelerator operated by Second Century Ventures, described as the most active venture fund in the global real estate technology space. CREtech, which hosts the sector's premier real estate AI conference drawing 3,000 leaders and 150 speakers annually, and CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, serve as the community and research nodes tracking proptech capital deployment and strategy.

Deployment considerations for firms evaluating AI entry points should begin with regulatory exposure. Any use of valuation models in mortgage or securitization decisions now requires conformance to federal quality control standards. For operational tools, the evidence points toward ROI in communication automation and data consolidation rather than accuracy gains on hard predictions. EliseAI, Building Engines, and Prophia position their value in time savings and workflow streamlining. The sector publishes model methodologies more transparently than most—Zillow and Redfin disclose Zestimate architecture and error rates openly, and Matterport, HouseCanary, and others detail their data sources and integration points. Firms should scrutinize whether claimed cost reductions in production cases come from labor displacement, faster cycle times, or better decision inputs, as vendor claims often blur these mechanisms. The BOMA trade association and NAR remain the clearest sources for profession-wide adoption patterns and best practices.
